opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I love those experiments, because they're so simple and so unsettling at the same time. For anyone who hasn't come across them: Petter Johansson and Lars Hall would show people two photographs of faces and ask which one they found more attractive. Then, using a bit of sleight of hand, they'd slide across the photo the person *didn't* choose and ask them to explain their choice. Most of the time people didn't notice the swap. And they would happily give reasons, often quite detailed ones. "I liked her earrings," when the face they'd actually picked had no earrings at all. They later did the same thing with jam and tea tastings, and even with political opinions on a survey, and got similar results.

What I take from that is that the narrator in our heads isn't a reporter with privileged access to the machinery of the decision. It's more like a press secretary, or, to be a bit more generous, an interpreter. It's constantly building a plausible, coherent story about why "I" did what I did, and it uses the same kinds of inference we'd use to explain someone else's behavior. Gazzaniga saw something very similar with split-brain patients decades ago. The left hemisphere would confidently confabulate explanations for actions that were actually driven by information only the right hemisphere had seen.

But I don't think the right conclusion is the cynical one, that our reasons are just fake and the "real" causes are hidden somewhere else. I'd frame it in terms of prediction and modeling. We are fundamentally social animals, and a huge part of what our brains do is model other minds: what they want, what they'll do next, why they did what they did. At some point, the same modeling machinery got turned on ourselves. Your sense of self is, in a sense, a theory of mind pointed inward. It's a model. And like any model, it's usually pretty good and occasionally wrong, and when it's wrong it doesn't announce that it's wrong. It just produces the most plausible output given what it can see.

The other thing that's interesting is that the stories aren't just epiphenomenal. In some of the follow-up work, once people had argued for the choice they hadn't actually made, they tended to stick with it later. The explanation became a kind of commitment. So the story isn't only a description of the self, it's partly constitutive of it. We author ourselves through these narratives, and then we live up to them, more or less.

And this is part of why I find the current debates about large language models a bit funny. People will say, "When a model explains its reasoning, it's just generating a plausible post-hoc rationalization, it doesn't have real access to why it produced that output." And it's like, well, yes, and Johansson's work suggests that's a pretty good description of us, too, a lot of the time. That doesn't mean the two are identical. But it should make us more humble about drawing a bright line where introspection is concerned. The gap between the process and the story about the process seems to be a feature of minds that model themselves, not a bug unique to machines.

r001.rationale: It says people were shown the photo they did not choose and then gave detailed reasons for choosing it.

r002.rationale: It says people tended to stick with the choice later and that the explanation became a commitment.

r003.rationale: It describes explanations confabulated by the left hemisphere for actions driven by information available only to the right hemisphere.

r004.rationale: It says the narrator builds a plausible, coherent story, but does not state that these justifications serve to preserve the impression of a single unified self.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I love those experiments, because they're such a clean demonstration of something that I think is deeply true about us, which is that the story and the choice are two different processes, and the story comes after.

Just to recap for people who don't know the work: Johansson and Lars Hall would show subjects two photographs of faces and ask them to pick the more attractive one. Then, with a bit of sleight of hand, they'd slide the rejected photo across the table and ask, "So why did you choose this one?" And most of the time people didn't notice the swap. Not only that, they'd confabulate. They'd say, "Well, I liked her earrings," or "He has a kinder expression," about a face they had just rejected a few seconds earlier. And they did it fluently, with the same confidence and the same detail as when they were explaining a choice they had actually made.

So the natural reaction is to say, aha, we're all deluded, introspection is a lie, the self is a fiction. And there's some truth in that, but I think the more interesting interpretation is less deflationary. What the experiment shows is that we have a narrator. We have a system whose job is to produce a coherent account of what the organism is doing, and that narrator is not in the loop on most of the decisions. It gets the outputs, and it does its best to explain them. It's a model of yourself, running inside yourself, and like all models it's lossy and it's sometimes wrong.

This connects to Gazzaniga's split-brain work from decades earlier, where the left hemisphere, the "interpreter," would invent reasons for actions that the right hemisphere had initiated. Same phenomenon. And I'd argue it's not a bug. If you're a social animal, you need to be able to give an account of yourself to others. You need to be predictable, legible, somebody that other people can model. The story we tell about our choices is really a story we tell to each other, and it's been internalized. So the narrator is doing a social job, not a forensic one. It's not trying to get the causal history right. It's trying to produce a self that hangs together.

And that's where I think it gets relevant to the things we're all thinking about now with language models. People say, "The model doesn't really know why it said that, it's just generating a plausible explanation." And yes, that's true. But that's also what we do. When you ask a large model why it produced an answer, you're asking its narrator, and its narrator has the same relationship to the underlying computation that ours does: partial access, plausible reconstruction. I don't think that makes the explanation worthless in either case. I think it means we should understand explanations, human or machine, as a kind of modeling, a compression, rather than as a readout.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that this means there's "no one home." The choice-blindness subject still made a choice. There was a real process that picked face A. There's also a real process that said "I liked the earrings." They just weren't the same process, and they're not fully transparent to each other. That's not the absence of a self. That's just what a self is, when it's made of many parts that have to coordinate without perfect information about each other. Which, honestly, is the only kind of self that could evolve.

r001.rationale: It describes subjects confabulating reasons for a face they had actually rejected after the experimenters swapped the photos.

r002.rationale: It discusses narratives explaining past choices, but does not say those narratives influence future choices.

r003.rationale: It says the narrator is not involved in most decisions and receives their outputs, distinguishing explanation from choice-making.

r004.rationale: It describes the narrator as producing a self that “hangs together,” linking explanations to a coherent sense of self.

astra-6.text:
I think they suggest that we have much less access to the causes of our own choices than we imagine. In Johansson’s experiments, someone makes a choice, and then, through a sleight of hand, they’re presented with the option they didn’t choose and asked to explain why they chose it. Often they don’t notice the switch. They offer a perfectly plausible explanation for a decision they never made.

That’s striking because they’re not necessarily lying. They’re doing something quite ordinary: looking at the situation and constructing an account that makes sense. We experience that account as introspection, as though we’re reading off the process that produced the choice. But it can be an interpretation made afterward.

I wouldn’t conclude that all our reasons are false or that choices don’t matter. It’s more that the story we tell about ourselves isn’t a transparent record of what happened. And that story can itself influence what happens next. If I explain a choice by saying, ‘I’m the kind of person who values this,’ that may shape my subsequent choices. So the narrative can be both an unreliable explanation of the past and a real influence on the future.

r001.rationale: It says people may explain a decision they never made after failing to notice a choice switch.

r002.rationale: It states that the story about a choice can shape subsequent choices.

r003.rationale: It describes explanations as post hoc interpretations, but does not suggest that distinct brain systems make choices and produce verbal explanations.

r004.rationale: It says explanations make sense of a situation, but does not explain them as preserving the impression of a unified self.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find so striking about Peter Johansson’s experiments is how readily we can explain a choice we didn’t actually make. You choose one of two faces, say, and through a sleight of hand you’re presented with the other one and asked why you chose it. Often you don’t notice the substitution. You just give reasons.

And those reasons can be perfectly coherent. So coherence isn’t evidence that we’ve accurately recovered the causes of our own behavior. We tend to imagine that we first have a reason, then make a choice, and finally report the reason. But sometimes the choice comes first, and the explanation is constructed afterward.

That doesn’t mean all our reasons are false, or that deliberation does nothing. It means introspection isn’t a transparent window onto the machinery producing our actions. The story we tell about ourselves is itself something the brain is doing. And that story can matter: even if it doesn’t faithfully explain the last choice, it can shape the next one.

r001.rationale: It describes someone explaining a choice they did not actually make after the face substitution goes unnoticed.

r002.rationale: It says the story about a past choice can shape the next choice.

r003.rationale: It says explanations may be constructed after choices, but does not clearly state that different brain systems produce the explanation and make the choice.

r004.rationale: It does not say that confabulated justifications preserve an impression of a single unified self.
